beats.say: A model predicts a short wait, and the request takes longer. Here it predicts two extra milliseconds; the server measures six. How could that one mistake teach the model to make a better prediction?

We'll follow this request through a learning step. The useful surprise is that a large network can share the same small calculation across every weight. Before we update anything, predict whether raising the weight and bias will raise or lower this positive-input prediction. Later we will change the input and test that reasoning again.

Our small model multiplies a complexity score by a weight, then adds a bias. The weight changes sensitivity to the input; the bias shifts every prediction. These are synthetic measurements, chosen so we can check the entire update.

Subtract the measured latency from the prediction. That signed residual is negative four. Squaring it gives a positive penalty, and taking half makes the derivative simpler. The loss is eight square milliseconds.
Imagine nudging the prediction a little toward the observation. Watch the point move down the loss curve. A slope tells us how much the loss changes for a small change in the prediction.
Here that slope is negative four. Increasing the prediction reduces the loss. Now give the weight and bias equal tiny nudges. Which one moves this prediction farther?

The weight's nudge gets multiplied by the input, so its effect is twice as large. Multiply those sensitivities along each path: the weight gradient is negative eight, and the bias gradient is negative four. A gradient measures local influence on the loss.

Backpropagation organizes that calculation as a graph. First compute forward and save the inputs needed by the local derivative rules. Each operation has a small job, even when the whole model is enormous. Visit each output before its parents in reverse topological order. Saving intermediates costs memory; checkpointing recomputes selected forward work to reduce that storage.

Start at the scalar loss with a derivative of one. The half-square multiplies the incoming signal by the saved residual. Subtracting the fixed target passes that signal unchanged toward the prediction.

Addition sends the signal to both inputs. The bias path is finished. The multiplication rule uses our saved input on the weight path. One reverse sweep shares this work across all the parameters connected to the loss.
Gradient descent moves against each local slope. The learning rate controls how far. With a rate of one tenth, both parameters move together using the gradients from the original forward pass.

Run the request through the updated model. The weight change adds most of the improvement, and the bias supplies the rest. Prediction rises to four: half the original gap, and a quarter of the original loss. We can now explain where that improvement came from.

We can check a custom backward rule independently. Hold the bias fixed and evaluate the loss with the weight nudged a little each way. Divide the loss difference by the distance between those two weights.

The numerical slope agrees with our backward result. This costs extra forward passes for each checked parameter, so it's useful for verification. Use double precision and smooth points; extremely tiny nudges can disappear into rounding. A large nudge can add approximation error; centered differences happen to be exact for our quadratic in exact arithmetic, but other objectives need not share that property.

Use an explicitly isolated micro-example to inspect shared ownership. A parameter can be used more than once. In a times a, both multiplication slots refer to the same value. Changing that value changes both slots.
Each path sends back a contribution of three. Add the first contribution, then the second. The shared derivative is six. This is why backward rules add into a gradient buffer whenever paths meet.

PyTorch keeps parameter gradient buffers across calls too. Recompute this forward pass and run backward again: the buffer reaches twelve. Clear before starting a new update, or accumulate deliberately across micro-batches at unchanged parameters. The article’s small scalar engine instead clears every reachable buffer at each backward call. Both implementations add contributions within one sweep. Keep parameter data unchanged between the saved forward and backward, then build a fresh graph after an update.

Dense layers use the same multiplication rule in arrays. Pair every incoming error component with every saved input to form the weight-gradient matrix. The bias receives the incoming signal, and the transposed weight matrix sends a signal toward earlier layers.

ReLU consults the saved preactivation. A positive input passes the incoming gradient; a negative input blocks it. At zero, this implementation chooses zero. The forward state decides which backward paths remain open. The ordinary derivative is undefined at exactly zero. A unit inactive on every example receives no gradient through this activation, while upstream changes or optimizer state can still change its inputs or parameters.

Max pooling saves the winning location. During backward, the incoming gradient goes to that location, including its sign. The other cells receive zero from this window. If windows overlap, their contributions add. Ties require an explicit winner convention; this example chooses the first maximum in row-major order.

These rules fit into five familiar steps. Clear the old gradients, compute predictions, reduce their errors to a scalar loss, and run backward. Up to this point, the parameter values have stayed fixed. Clearing to None leaves an untouched parameter with no gradient, so the optimizer skips it. A zero-valued tensor can still participate in an update through optimizer state or regularization. Backward normally releases saved tensors, so keeping the loss reference does not make repeating that same backward valid.
The optimizer step changes the parameters. A new forward pass then measures the new prediction. The step leaves the gradient buffers in place, so the next effective batch begins by clearing them.

For validation, switch modules to evaluation behavior and disable reverse-mode recording. Evaluation mode changes layers such as dropout; no-grad controls graph recording. Return to training mode before the next training batch. Dropout becomes the identity. Batch normalization uses stored running estimates by default, but configurations without running estimates still use batch statistics. No-grad controls the current thread’s reverse-mode recording; it does not change existing requires-grad flags or disable forward-mode differentiation.

Let's train on three requests, starting from zero weight and bias. A mean loss gives every request one third of the influence. Full-batch descent waits for all the data; online descent steps after one example. Mini-batches combine several examples per step.

Suppose memory allows two requests, then one. Weight each chunk mean by its share of the examples. Accumulate at the same parameters, and take one step after both chunks. Each request keeps the same influence as in the full mean. This equivalence assumes a deterministic sum of independent per-example losses. Training-mode batch normalization can change the forward computation when a batch is split. For a masked token mean, weight each chunk mean by its valid-token count over the effective total, not its number of requests.

Giving each chunk half the weight overemphasizes the lone request. Autograd follows the objective we wrote. Count the denominator of the actual loss, and validate the learning rate when batch size changes. Batch-dependent layers can also change the computation when a batch is split. Uniform independent sampling makes a mean mini-batch gradient unbiased for that full gradient and divides its covariance by batch size. The update count still changes: sixty presentations of six examples make ten full-batch, thirty two-example, or sixty online updates. Measure validation behavior and throughput before choosing a batch size.

Return to our original request. Moving both parameters changes its prediction through two paths. Together they multiply the old residual by one minus five times the learning rate. The input scale is part of that factor. For general input x in this affine half-squared example, the residual multiplier is one minus the learning rate times the quantity x squared plus one.

Watch repeated updates. At one tenth, the gap halves each time. One fifth lands exactly on this target. A rate of one half overshoots, flips the residual, and makes the next gap larger. A correct derivative still needs a sensible step size. At exactly point four, the residual flips without shrinking. For this nonzero-residual quadratic, convergence requires the rate strictly between zero and point four. One example also leaves many parameter pairs with the same fitted prediction.

A gradient describes influence, so the input sign matters too. Reverse the input and the initial weight together, keeping the same prediction. The weight now moves downward, and the prediction still rises toward the observation.

A deep network repeats these local multiplications. Follow one backward signal through five contracting layers. Early layers receive very little. Repeated expansion has the opposite effect: the signal grows as it travels. Real layer Jacobians can treat different directions differently.
For an oversized finite gradient, norm clipping applies one common scale. This vector has length ten. Bring it to a limit of five: both coordinates shrink together, so the direction stays the same.

Clip the accumulated gradient after backward and before the optimizer step. With mixed-precision scaling, unscale first. Nonfinite values require finding the numerical failure upstream, and an adaptive optimizer can further change the final update.

Initialization sets the signal scale before the first update. Independent, centered inputs contribute variances that add. With many inputs, unscaled weights can create a huge spread. Scaling the weight variance inversely with fan-in keeps that sum controlled.

Xavier balances forward fan-in and backward fan-out for roughly linear, centered activations. For equal-width layers, its weight variance is one over the width. Random, independently initialized weights also let hidden units learn different roles. More generally the gain-one Xavier variance is two divided by fan-in plus fan-out. Its normal standard deviation is the square root of that variance; a symmetric uniform distribution uses endpoints plus and minus the square root of six over fan-in plus fan-out. Different outgoing weights can already break the symmetry of units with equal incoming weights; zero biases with independent weights are common.

Look back at our first checked update. We can follow its error backward, explain each parameter's influence, and verify the next prediction. That same bookkeeping makes a large neural network trainable, one measured step at a time.
